title: Secure the Perimeter
blurb: A budget, a shop of real controls, one network. Place your defenses, then watch three attack waves resolve against what each control can actually do.
source: Concepts per ISC2 CISSP Official Study Guide, 10th edition, ch.11 (Secure Network Architecture) and ch.12 (Secure Communications); April-2024 exam outline areas 4.1-4.2

siege.title: Secure the Perimeter
siege.prompt: One network, three attack waves, one budget for the whole night. Every control in the shop lists what it can actually do — attacks resolve against those properties, not against the control's name.
siege.hint: The full-coverage build exists and costs exactly par. Cheap now can be expensive later: the wave-2 traffic remembers what the wave-1 bargain could not see.

chips.label: Packet-filter firewall
chips.definition: First-generation rule list: permits or drops each packet by source, destination, and port, one packet at a time, with no memory of any conversation.
chips.why: A static packet filter is the cheapest gate at a choke point, but because it inspects packets in isolation it cannot tell a legitimate reply from an unsolicited flood — state-based attacks walk past it.

chips.label: Stateful inspection firewall
chips.definition: Third-generation firewall: tracks every conversation in a state table, so a packet is judged by the connection it belongs to, not just its header fields.
chips.why: Keeping a state table is what lets a firewall drop half-open floods and unsolicited traffic that a stateless rule list would wave through — the classic upgrade at the perimeter choke point.

chips.label: Next-generation firewall
chips.definition: Deep-packet appliance: everything the stateful firewall does, plus application awareness and outbound traffic control in a single (expensive) box.
chips.why: An NGFW identifies the application inside the flow rather than trusting the port number, and can police egress — breadth in one seat, at a price that forces a budget decision.

chips.label: Web application firewall
chips.definition: Sits in front of a web server and reads the HTTP payload itself — queries, parameters, headers — blocking requests whose content attacks the application.
chips.why: Port 443 is legitimately open, so packet, stateful, and even application-identifying firewalls pass a well-formed HTTPS request; only payload inspection sees the injection inside it. That is the WAF's whole job.

chips.label: Signature NIPS
chips.definition: Inline network intrusion prevention matching traffic against a database of known attack patterns. Blocks what it recognizes — and only what it recognizes.
chips.why: Signature detection is precise and cheap against published attacks, and an inline placement can block rather than merely alert. Its blind spot is definitional: an attack with no signature yet does not match anything.

chips.label: Anomaly-based NIPS
chips.definition: Inline prevention that learns a baseline of normal traffic and blocks significant deviations — no signature required, more tuning required.
chips.why: Anomaly detection is the counter to novel attacks: it flags behavior that departs from the baseline instead of looking up a pattern, which is exactly what a zero-day never has.

chips.label: Forward proxy
chips.definition: Terminates outbound connections on behalf of internal hosts: nothing inside talks to the internet directly, and the proxy logs, filters, and can refuse every request.
chips.why: Mediating egress is the control that catches traffic leaving — beaconing malware included. Inbound-facing defenses never see an outbound channel; a proxy exists on exactly that path.

chips.label: Switch security bundle
chips.definition: VLAN segmentation plus 802.1X port authentication on the switch fabric: traffic is fenced into segments, and a device must authenticate before its wall port carries anything.
chips.why: Segmentation decides how far one compromised host can reach, and port-based network access control decides whether an unknown device gets a link at all — both live in the switch, not at the perimeter.

chips.label: Mail security gateway
chips.definition: Scrubs inbound mail before the relay accepts it: attachment detonation, link rewriting, spoofing checks, and sender authentication.
chips.why: Mail rides its own protocol path into the DMZ, so web- and port-focused controls never inspect it; a dedicated gateway on the mail seat is what stands between a lure and an inbox.

chips.label: Hardened server baseline
chips.definition: The unglamorous control: unnecessary services removed, default credentials gone, patches current, configuration locked to a documented baseline.
chips.why: Hardening shrinks the attack surface itself, so an exploit aimed at a service that is disabled, patched, or locked down has nothing to land on — protection that does not depend on recognizing the attack.

events.failCopy: The choke point had no filter, so the sweep walked every port into the DMZ and came back with a map of your web server.
events.stopCopy: The filter at the choke point dropped the probes — closed ports stayed silent and the sweep mapped nothing.
events.why: A firewall at the perimeter choke point is the control that answers scanning: any deny-by-default filter makes closed ports invisible instead of chatty.

events.failCopy: Port 443 is supposed to be open, so every port-level control waved the request through — the injection rode a legal channel to the database behind the web tier.
events.stopCopy: The payload inspector read the query string, recognized the injection pattern, and refused the request before the application saw it.
events.why: An application-layer attack arrives inside allowed traffic; only a control that inspects the HTTP payload itself — a WAF — can tell a malicious request from a legitimate one on the same port.

events.failCopy: The relay accepted the lure untouched, a user did what users do, and the dropper detonated on an endpoint three hops inside your perimeter.
events.stopCopy: The mail gateway detonated the attachment in a sandbox, saw the dropper, and the lure never reached an inbox.
events.why: Mail enters on its own protocol path, so firewalls tuned for web traffic never read it; a mail security gateway on that path is the control that stops the lure before a human can click it.

events.failCopy: Each packet looked innocent on its own, and packets-on-their-own is all a stateless filter can see — the half-open flood exhausted the web tier behind it.
events.stopCopy: The state table saw thousands of half-open handshakes that never completed and dropped the flood at the boundary.
events.why: A SYN flood is invisible to per-packet rules because every packet is individually well-formed; only connection-state tracking notices that the handshakes never finish.

events.failCopy: Nothing on the switch fabric was reading the traffic, so a worm with a published signature crossed the core unchallenged and started on the workstations.
events.stopCopy: The sensor on the core matched the propagation traffic against its database and blocked a worm the whole industry already had a name for.
events.why: A published, fingerprinted attack is signature detection's home game: cheap, precise, and low-noise — the economical pick when the threat is known.

events.attackClass: Lateral movement across a flat LAN
events.failCopy: The LAN was one flat broadcast domain, so a single compromised host could reach the server rack directly — nothing between it and the crown jewels but cable.
events.stopCopy: The VLAN fences held: the compromised segment could not route to the server segment, and the pivot died at the switch.
events.why: Segmentation is the control that decides blast radius — perimeter devices never see east-west traffic, so the fence has to live in the switch fabric itself.

events.failCopy: No signature exists for an attack published nowhere, so pattern-matching defenses had nothing to match — the exploit landed on a listening service and the rack answered to someone else.
events.stopCopy: There was no signature to match — but the target surface had been hardened away, and the anomalous behavior that remained stood out from the baseline and was blocked.
events.why: A zero-day defeats signature databases by definition; what answers it is reducing the surface it needs (hardening) or flagging the deviation it causes (anomaly detection) — recognition of the attack is never available.

events.attackClass: Rogue device on a wall port
events.failCopy: The wall port carried traffic for anything that plugged in, so an unmanaged box joined the LAN with the same standing as a corporate laptop.
events.stopCopy: The port challenged the device for credentials it did not have — 802.1X left the intruder holding a dead link.
events.why: Port-based network access control (802.1X) authenticates the device before the port passes traffic; without it, physical access to a socket is network access.

events.failCopy: Everything watched the front door while the beacon left through the back: outbound HTTPS flowed unmediated, and the implant checked in with its operator on schedule.
events.stopCopy: Outbound connections had to justify themselves to the proxy, and a rhythmic call to an eleven-day-old domain did not — the channel died before the first tasking arrived.
events.why: Inbound-facing controls never inspect the outbound path; egress mediation is the distinct control that catches command-and-control traffic leaving the network.

events.failCopy: Nothing filtered the choke point, and the sweep mapped the DMZ.
events.stopCopy: The demo firewall on the choke point dropped the probes — this is what an interception looks like.
events.why: A deny-by-default filter at the choke point makes closed ports invisible to scanning.

events.failCopy: The web server had no payload inspection, so the injection rode legal HTTPS straight through — watch the breach path: this is what an unguarded seat costs.
events.stopCopy: Payload inspection refused the request before the application saw it.
events.why: Application-layer attacks arrive inside allowed traffic; only payload inspection on the web seat answers them.
